2026年的中国算力市场，正经历一场剧烈分化：一边是头部企业订单排期至2028年、净利润暴涨超800%的火热景象；另一边，则是西部大量中小玩家在利用率不足70%的亏损线上挣扎，部分智算中心甚至烂尾。

...

她提醒，当前算力市场最大的泡沫在于“供需错配下的非理性溢价”与“重资产金融化”。部分企业甚至将GPU（图形处理器）作为抵押物进行高杠杆融资，形成类似“贷款炒房”的算力地产模式。

...

胡蓉： 当前算力市场真正火的是高端智算领域，尤其是大模型训练和推理所需的算力，企业需求量大，但受各种因素影响往往出现严重的供不应求问题，导致部分显卡租赁价格暴涨。资金雄厚的头部企业提前布局好相关算力资源，在租赁市场不缺下家，自然有充足的利润空间。但针对算力资源的投建布局应做出合理规划，做到物尽其用，才不至于陷入供需不匹配的困境。

早期的算力租赁市场存在粗放式暴利，谁先拿到显卡、谁就能以天价出租，这是供需极度错配下的阶段性红利。随着更多资本涌入、更多数据中心投产，单纯靠资源差价赚取超额利润的窗口确实在收窄。

但2026年“进场”仍有大机会，只是机会的性质变了。算力行业应该从“租资源”向“卖服务”迈进。机会主要在三个方面：第一，构建差异化的生态能力，比如围绕特定行业提供定制化算力解决方案；第二，抓住推理需求爆发的结构性机遇，围绕推理场景提供精细化调度、成本优化、按需服务等深度运营能力；第三，紧跟国内算力行业发展趋势，比如建立起Token（人工智能模型处理文字时的最小单位）运营的能力。暴利期或许过去了，但价值创造期刚刚开始。

经济观察报：当前算力市场最大的泡沫在哪里？最危险的信号是什么？

胡蓉： 最大的泡沫在于“供需错配下的非理性溢价”与“重资产金融化”。例如B300服务器价格一度飙升到700万元、租赁价暴涨40%，其核心驱动力并非单纯的技术需求，而是叠加了海外出口管制、合规渠道受阻及灰色市场炒作等多重因素。部分企业甚至将GPU作为抵押物进行高杠杆融资，形成类似“贷款炒房”的算力地产模式，导致资产估值严重脱离实际商业回报。

最危险的信号是“技术迭代推迟引发的资产贬值风险”与“下游商业化变现受阻”。一旦新一代芯片因先进封装良率等问题延迟交付，或人工智能（AI）应用无法实现规模化盈利，高昂的算力成本将直接压垮下游客户。届时，高价囤积的旧款GPU将面临租金暴跌和流动性枯竭的双重打击，前期盲目扩张的重资产极易沦为不良债务，引发产业链的系统性出清。

...

胡蓉： 第一是网络时延的硬约束：长距离传输带来的时延问题对于实时性要求高的AI推理任务仍是难以逾越的壁垒；第二是技术标准与接口不统一：不同集群、不同厂商的数据中心在算力计量、计费方式、API（应用程序编程接口‌）接口、调度协议上各行其是，企业想同时使用多个区域的算力，往往需要做大量的适配开发，交易成本居高不下；第三是跨域服务保障难度大：算力跨省调用后，费用如何结算、服务质量如何保障、故障责任如何界定，目前缺乏统一规则。

...

胡蓉： 国产算力和英伟达之间确实存在差距，核心在软件生态。英伟达的CUDA（GPU 通用计算开发平台）生态成熟、工具链完善，开发者上手快、迁移成本低，这些正是国产算力需要完善的地方。不过这种差距正在缩小，目前主流国产芯片在推理场景中已具备不错的竞争力，成本控制空间更大。差距主要集中于超大规模训练场景的单卡性能和集群稳定性，但通过系统优化和调度提升，这一差距正在逐步缩小。

results.title: Wuhu Big Data warns of Chinese GPU rental market bubbles
highlights:
Wuhu Big Data Chairman Hu Rong warns of bubbles in China's 2026 computing power market, citing risky 'computing power real estate' financing models.

The Chinese computing power market is experiencing severe divergence in 2026, characterized by irrational premiums and risky financialization of heavy assets. While top-tier providers have order books filled through 2028 and report net profit surges exceeding 800%, many small and medium-sized players in western regions are struggling. These smaller data centers often face utilization rates below 70%, operating under loss lines with some intelligent computing projects remaining unfinished. Hu Rong, Chairman of Wuhu Big Data Construction, Investment and Operation Co., Ltd., highlighted significant bubbles within the current computing power rental market. A key concern is the creation of a 'computing power real estate' model, where companies use Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) as collateral for high-leverage financing. She warned that the era of crude, excess profits solely from resource price differences is closing, urging a shift from simply renting resources to providing deep operational services. Wuhu holds a unique position as one of the two major hubs in the Yangtze River Delta under China's 'East Data West Computing' national strategy and is the only national-level data center cluster in central China. The cluster hosts major projects from Huawei, Douyin, and the top three telecom carriers, handling over 70% of Anhui province's intelligent computing tasks. Wuhu Big Data, a local state-owned asset platform, is addressing these market challenges by operating a provincial-level computing power dispatch and trading platform. Instead of acting merely as a 'rack landlord,' the company utilizes a light-asset model aimed at making computing power flow as efficiently as water or electricity, facilitating cross-regional trading. The biggest risks facing the sector include asset devaluation triggered by delayed technology iterations, such as chip delivery issues, and blocked downstream AI commercialization. If high-priced, older GPU models face rent crashes and liquidity drainage due to these factors, it could lead to systemic industry clearance. Wuhu mitigates this by diversifying revenue through platform fees, data operations, and ecosystem benefits rather than relying on pure asset leasing.

results.title: Is the AI-Cost Floor About to Lift? · FDE.build
highlights:
Two facts are both true, and almost never stated in the same breath. The price you pay for a token has collapsed. Epoch AI puts the decline at somewhere between 9 and 900 times a year, depending on the task, with a median around 50 times annually over the three years to March 2025. And the companies charging that price are losing money on most of what they serve. Will Sommer, a senior director analyst at Gartner, put it plainly in remarks to CIO Dive, reported in March 2026. The largest labs, he said, "are not making money right now: They're losing money."

...

This article is not a forecast that prices are about to rise. The long-run trend points down, and it points down hard. But a falling average is fully compatible with the floor lifting for a few quarters along the way. ... Treat it as a risk to absorb, not a prediction to bet on.

...

A provider that wanted to serve you more cheaply would still have to buy the hardware to do it, and the hardware is pre-committed.

The bottleneck is not the chip die. It is the memory and the packaging around it. The advanced packaging that high-end accelerators depend on was roughly 70 percent pre-committed to a single customer, NVIDIA, for 2025 capacity, according to Techverx. High-bandwidth memory is worse. SK Hynix's finance chief said the company has already sold out its entire 2026 HBM supply. Micron's chief executive said its memory capacity for 2025 and 2026 is fully booked. Demand for that memory is growing 80 to 100 percent a year against supply growth of 50 to 60 percent.

The downstream effect is visible in lead times and prices. Data-centre GPU lead times now run 36 to 52 weeks from resellers, and AWS raised H200 instance pricing by 15 percent in January 2026 alone. VerticalData's summary of the procurement reality is blunt: hardware availability, not engineering readiness, is often the gating factor for AI projects. When the hyperscalers absorb most of the allocation, everyone else is buying from a thinner pool at a higher clearing price.

## Power is the harder ceiling

Chips you can eventually fabricate. The constraint that resists capital is the grid.

The numbers are stark. Against roughly 16 gigawatts of announced United States data-centre pipeline for 2026, only about 5 gigawatts is actually under construction. Tech Insider reports that 30 to 50 percent of planned projects are expected to slip or be cancelled. There is a five-year backlog on grid transformers. Connecting a new facility to the grid can take 4 to 10 years, against the 2 to 3 years it takes to build the data centre itself. Morgan Stanley projects United States data-centre demand reaching about 74 gigawatts by 2028, with a shortfall of roughly 49 gigawatts in available power. The World Economic Forum, writing in May 2026, named grid connectivity, not silicon, as the strategic bottleneck for AI.

This matters for pricing because it is a constraint you cannot capital-spend your way out of inside eighteen months. A shortage of chips eases when the fabrication line catches up. A shortage of grid interconnects holds for years. A constraint that holds is a constraint that can hold a price floor up with it.

...

The honest part is that a lift rarely arrives as a headline price rise. It arrives sideways. It looks like quota caps and rate limits. It looks like throttling. UncoverAlpha has noted that Claude users have already reported throttling during peak demand. It looks like the quiet deprecation of the cheap older model you built on, nudging you towards a pricier current one. Above all, it looks like the death of the flat-rate, unlimited tier. One analyst at UncoverAlpha made this point directly: you can offer a 20-dollar-a-month unlimited plan that costs 100 dollars a month to serve only while you are private and burning venture capital. The same analyst's conclusion is the sharpest statement of the risk. The math only works if prices go up, or if the compute infrastructure grows fast enough to meet demand, which it cannot in the short term. Name these forms now, so you recognise the floor lifting even when no list price changes.

results.title: AI Infrastructure’s Bottleneck Shifts from Chips to Power: The Grid Paradox
highlights:
Hyperscalers and cloud providers are discovering that the real ceiling for AI expansion isn’t compute, it’s electricity. While NVIDIA’s Blackwell and AMD’s MI350X promise unprecedented performance, the North American data center market faces a structural power deficit that could throttle growth. Industry reports now peg 2028 IT power demand at nearly 90 GW, a 30% jump from today, yet grid upgrades lag by years. The result is a market where hardware advances outpace infrastructure readiness, forcing operators to prioritize power procurement over GPU procurement.

...

Data center operators are racing to secure power contracts before AI buildouts accelerate, but grid operators and utilities can’t keep ... Hyperscalers are now prioritizing campus-scale infrastructure, locking in land and interconnection agreements years in advance to guarantee power access.

...

## Secondary GPU Markets Hint at Supply Saturation

Despite ongoing GPU shortages in some segments, the secondary market for used H100 accelerators remains tight. Mordor Intelligence reports that resale values for older-generation cards hold firm due to sustained demand, with supply trailing by up to 40%. Yet this isn’t a sign of persistent scarcity. Instead, it signals a market adjusting to a new reality where hyperscalers are no longer desperate for raw compute, they’re constrained by power, cooling, and integration challenges. The high resale values for H100s contrast with the cooling-off in GPU rental markets, as reported by Data Center Knowledge, where pricing pressure is easing in segments where new capacity has come online.

The secondary market’s resilience also reflects a strategic shift among cloud providers. Rather than chasing the latest GPUs, operators are optimizing existing clusters for efficiency, prolonging the lifespan of older hardware. This approach reduces capex pressure while allowing hyperscalers to focus capital on power infrastructure. The trend is particularly pronounced among smaller cloud providers and AI startups, which lack the balance sheets to compete in new GPU procurement.

results.title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on IPO, Compute Scarcity, and a New Device
highlights:
- Compute through 2027 is gone. OpenAI’s CFO confirmed no additional compute is available through 2026 and most of 2027; she is already securing capacity for 2030-2032.
- The $122B March raise is the largest private fundraise in history. The IPO is a milestone when convenient - not a race against Anthropic’s S1 filing.
- OpenAI’s unit economics: 900M weekly ChatGPT users, 97% compute cost deflation from GPT-4 to GPT-5.4, revenue approaching 50/50 consumer/enterprise, Codex at 5M users since January 2026.
- A new consumer hardware device from Johnny Ive’s team will be unveiled by end of 2026. Friar has tried it, calls it “very lovable,” and sat on her hands to avoid describing it on camera.

The IPO Waits. The Compute Won’t.

Compute for 2026 is gone. Sarah Friar confirmed it on air - and said she is already buying compute for 2030.

That framing - not the IPO question, not the Anthropic rivalry - is the structural signal in this interview. Everything else Sarah says flows from it: why the $122B raise happened, why the IPO is not scheduled, why the Michigan data center matters, and what the revenue path looks like across the next decade.

results.title: Wasted GPU capacity is a real business now — The Lede
highlights:
Expanse, a YC P26 company, launched on HN today with a pitch built around one specific fact: data centers run at 30-40% effective utilization. Their product tries to unlock that idle capacity. The thread got into the weeds on why data centers do not just pass the savings to customers directly, and the answer is basically that tiered pricing is hard to build and burst demand is unpredictable.

This sits alongside the Groq thread, where fast inference is being positioned as a premium worth paying for. The through-line is that the GPU market is bifurcating. On one end, you have companies trying to arbitrage underutilized capacity for cheaper compute. On the other, you have companies charging a premium for speed and reliability. Both are real businesses, but they serve different customers. The cheap-compute play is for batch workloads and training runs. The premium-inference play is for latency-sensitive production applications.

...

Founders building AI products need to think about compute costs as a first-class business variable, not an afterthought. The price gap between cheap burst capacity and premium inference is widening, and your product architecture should reflect which bucket you are in. If you are using AWS to access OpenAI because procurement is easier, you are paying a tax that a smaller competitor may not be paying.
